title: Which of these five statements about prime numbers are true?
description: Five statements about prime numbers are tested one at a time with a small example or a count of factors. Some turn out true and some false.
teaching_notes: One idea: a statement about prime numbers is judged by counting factors, and one example that breaks it is enough to make it false. Watch for students who say that all even numbers are composite.

video_script.why: The child tests each statement by counting factors, the way the book decides whether a number is prime or composite.
video_script.substitution: Test each statement with a small example and a count of factors.
video_script.anchor: Five statements on the board, each waiting to be marked true or false
video_script.payoff_line: The first and the last statements are true, and the other three are false.

final_answer.value: a True, b False, c False, d False, e True
final_answer.spoken: the first and last statements are true and the other three are false

maths_rules: a number with units digit 4 is even and bigger than 2, so it has the factors 1, 2 and itself; it is composite (14 = 2 × 7, 34 = 2 × 17)
2 × 3 = 6; factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3, 6; a product of primes has more than 2 factors
a prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, so it does have factors
2 is even and prime, so not all even numbers are composite
after a prime bigger than 2 comes an even number bigger than 2, which is composite: 5 then 6, 7 then 8, 11 then 12
video_script.design: Five statement cards; each is tested with a small example and then stamped true in teal or false in amber.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; five statement cards about prime numbers; true and false stamps

marks.cards: the five statement cards appear one below the other
marks.ask: the true and false stamps appear

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about prime numbers.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which of them are true, and which are false? Give a reason for each.

beats.on_screen: the five statement cards stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: Prime = exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Composite = more than two factors. One example that breaks a statement makes it false.

marks.break: an example that breaks a statement lights up

narration: <bookmark mark='prime'/>A prime number has exactly two factors, one and the number itself.
<bookmark mark='comp'/>A composite number has more than two factors.
<bookmark mark='break'/>One example that breaks a statement is enough to make it false.

beats.on_screen: Given: 1. no prime has units digit 4. 2. a product of primes can be prime. 3. primes have no factors. 4. all even numbers are composite. 5. after a prime comes a composite, except after 2

marks.given: the five statements are written in short form

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, five statements about prime numbers, as listed on the board.

beats.on_screen: To find: true or false for each, with a reason

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to mark each statement true or false and give a reason.

beats.on_screen: 1. A number ending in 4 is even: 14 = 2 × 7, 34 = 2 × 17, composite. True

marks.one: the first statement is tested with fourteen and thirty four
marks.stamp: the first statement is stamped true in teal

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step one, take the first statement. A number ending in four is even, such as fourteen, which is two times seven.
<bookmark mark='stamp'/>Two is a factor along with one and the number itself, so no such number is prime. The statement is true.

beats.on_screen: 2. 2 × 3 = 6, factors 1, 2, 3, 6: False. 3. a prime has the factors 1 and itself: False

marks.two: two times three is written with the factors of six
marks.three: the third statement is tested with the factors of seven and stamped false in amber

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, take the second statement. Two times three is six, and six has four factors, so it is composite. The statement is false.
<bookmark mark='three'/>For the third statement, seven has the factors one and seven, so a prime does have factors. That statement is false.

beats.on_screen: 4. 2 is even and prime: False. 5. after 5 comes 6, after 7 comes 8, after 11 comes 12: True

marks.four: the number two is shown as an even prime
marks.five: the pairs five and six, seven and eight, eleven and twelve are written
marks.stamp: the fourth statement is stamped false and the fifth true

narration: <bookmark mark='four'/>Step three, take the fourth statement. Two is even and also prime, so not every even number is composite. That statement is false.
<bookmark mark='five'/>For the fifth statement, look at what follows a prime bigger than two. It is an even number bigger than two, which is composite.
<bookmark mark='stamp'/>Five then six, seven then eight and eleven then twelve all fit. That statement is true.

beats.on_screen: Check: the five stamps are true, false, false, false, true

marks.check: the five stamps are lined up in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check the stamps. Each statement was decided with an example or a count of factors.

beats.on_screen: Answer: a True, b False, c False, d False, e True
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The first and the last statements are true, and the other three are false.
